subject: Huawei criminal trial verdict (2026)
title: Huawei verdict: What was it convicted of? Trade secrets and bank fraud
answer: On Tuesday, Nov. 24, 2026, a federal jury in Brooklyn found China's Huawei Technologies and three of its subsidiaries guilty on 10 of 12 counts, including conspiracy to steal trade secrets, bank fraud, wire fraud and violating U.S. sanctions on Iran. Jurors acquitted the company of racketeering conspiracy, the most serious charge.
in_the_news: The verdict closes a criminal case that began with the 2018 arrest of Huawei's finance chief in Canada and has shaped U.S.-China tech relations ever since. The company says it will appeal, and Beijing has already protested.
body:
The defendants were Huawei Technologies and three subsidiaries: Huawei Device Co., Futurewei Technologies and Huawei Device USA. Prosecutors told jurors the company misled banks including HSBC about its business in Iran, operated there through a subsidiary called Skycom, and spent two decades taking technology from American rivals. Court records name Cisco, Motorola Solutions, T-Mobile, Quintel USA and Fujitsu among the targets. Evidence at the trial included Cisco source code that ended up in Huawei routers, a piece of a T-Mobile phone-testing robot that an employee carried out of a lab, and a Huawei engineer photographing a device inside a Fujitsu booth at a trade show in Chicago. The trial lasted more than two months, with more than 60 prosecution witnesses.

Besides racketeering conspiracy, the jury acquitted on a charge of conspiring to obstruct justice. Defense attorney Brian Heberlig called the racketeering acquittal a rejection of the government's central narrative and said the company would appeal. In a statement on Wednesday, Huawei said the remaining convictions were equally without merit and that the trade secret disputes were civil matters settled years ago. China's Foreign Ministry said Beijing firmly opposes what it called U.S. suppression of Chinese companies. Attorney General Todd Blanche said the verdict showed that no person or company is above the law.

How the case got here: Dec. 1, 2018 — Huawei finance chief Meng Wanzhou, the founder's daughter, is arrested in Vancouver on a U.S. warrant. January 2019 — U.S. prosecutors unseal bank fraud and sanctions charges against the company. May 2019 — the Commerce Department adds Huawei to its trade blacklist, cutting it off from many American suppliers. June 2019 — in a separate civil case, a Texas jury finds Huawei took trade secrets from chip startup CNEX Labs but awards no damages. February 2020 — prosecutors add racketeering and trade secret conspiracy charges. September 2021 — Meng signs a deferred prosecution agreement acknowledging false statements about the Iran business and returns to China; her charges are later dropped. Nov. 24, 2026 — the jury verdict.

What comes next: a company cannot go to prison, so the penalties are financial. The Justice Department said Huawei faces criminal fines, forfeiture and restitution, with no amount announced yet. Fox Business reported that sentencing is scheduled for Sept. 14, 2027. Huawei can ask the trial judge to set aside the verdict and then appeal to the 2nd U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals. For American consumers, little changes right away: Huawei phones and network gear have been effectively shut out of the U.S. market for years.

faq.q: Will anyone from Huawei go to prison?
faq.a: No. The defendants are companies, not people, so the possible punishment is fines, forfeiture of money and restitution to victims. No individual executive was on trial.

faq.q: Can you still buy Huawei phones in the U.S.?
faq.a: Huawei has been on the U.S. trade blacklist since 2019 and is barred from selling equipment to U.S. carriers, so its phones are not sold through American carriers or major U.S. retailers. The verdict does not change that.

faq.q: Was Meng Wanzhou part of this trial?
faq.a: No. Meng returned to China in 2021 under a deferred prosecution agreement, and the charges against her were dropped. Prosecutors showed jurors the statement of facts she acknowledged in that agreement, but she did not testify.
Racketeering conspiracy, a charge more common in organized crime cases, and conspiracy to obstruct justice. The jury convicted on the other 10 counts.
